old_title: SpaceX launches most powerful rocket ever into orbit for first time - live updates
new_title: SpaceX's Starship dramatically explodes after first orbital trip

SpaceX has launched the world's most powerful rocket into orbit for the first ever time.
Elon Musk's private space company is conducting its 14th test flight of Starship, and the first to try and reach orbit.
The mission launched at 7.48am local central time, or 1.48pm in the UK, lifting off from SpaceX's "Starbase" facility in Texas.
The spacecraft suffered an engine failure, putting its trip into orbit in doubt, but SpaceX continued on its plan to deploy 26 Starlink space internet satellites. After orbiting the planet six times, Starship is then set to splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, roughly 10 hours after launch.
It is seen as a major test both of SpaceX's future plans and its role in helping Nasa return to the Moon and then onto Mars.
The whole launch is available to watch online and covered in detail on The Independent. Follow below for all the latest on the launch - and what it means for our plans to head into space.
Starship launch live stream
The official live stream for Starship Flight 14 is underway. You can watch it here:
First Starlink satellite deploys
Starship has deployed the first of 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The next 25 should pop out over the next 30 minutes.
These are the first operational Starlink satellites to make it to orbit aboard a Starship rocket, and will help rapidly expand the space internet network.
You can see the first Starlink satellite coming out of the hatch at the top of the image here:
Starship is orbital
Starship has made it to orbit! The engine burn was successful, marking a huge milestone for SpaceX. It is the first time the world's biggest and most powerful rocket has made it into orbit.
Next step will be getting 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.
'We are go for orbit'
SpaceX has changed its mind - it is now going to attempt to send Starship to orbit, even if one of its engines has failed.
"We are go for orbit," SpaceX says.
The news gets big cheers from the SpaceX ground crew.
Starship is going to coast through space for a few more minutes before the orbital burn is attempted. If successful, the next big step will be deploying the Starlink satellites into orbit.
SpaceX to make 'go/ no go' decision for orbital mission
The engine failure might not prevent Starship from reaching orbit. We're just waiting to hear the final decision from SpaceX...
BREAKING: Starship not heading to orbit
Due to that engine going out, SpaceX is no longer planning to send Starship to orbit.
"We are not going to do the additional burn that will send us into orbit," SpaceX says.
Super Heavy booster splashes down
The Super Heavy booster has splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico after separating from the upper stage Starship rocket.
It was a "fairly soft" splashdown, according to the SpaceX team, meaning it didn't explode as soon as it hit the water.
One of the Starship engines has failed, though it's continuing its mission to orbit. "We need to check in and see what exactly that means for the rest of the mission here," SpaceX says.
Stage separation complete
The upper stage has successfully separated from the Super Heavy booster.

SpaceX's Starship has been sent into orbit for the first ever time - before returning to Earth with an explosion at sea.
The spacecraft's 14th flight was seen as a critical test of Elon Musk's hopes to take humanity back to the Moon and Mars. And it largely succeeded, launching into orbit, deploying a set of Starlink satellites and then coming back down to Earth.
But that arrival back on our planet came with a dramatic fireball. The spacecraft successfully flipped itself around to land softly in the ocean - and then exploded in a huge fireball once it had hit the water.
Eventually, SpaceX hopes that Starship is able to conduct that same flip manoeuvre on land in Texas, so that it can safely carry people home and then be ready to be re-used. But for the moment, the spacecraft is being landed in the sea with no plan to recover and recycle it.
SpaceX shared video of the Starship's final moments and its splashdown from its official feed. But it notably cut the video before the explosion, which occurred very shortly after Starship had fallen into the ocean.
The mission had already been hit by a range of technical problems as it flew around Earth. Mid-flight, SpaceX spotted that one of Starship's engines shut down unexpectedly, and the journey had to be reduced from ten hours to three hours.
On SpaceX's live stream, spokespeople initially suggested that the problem would mean that the company would abandon its plan to send Starship into orbit for the first time. But after a range of conversations and checks, engineers confirmed that they would be able to boost it into orbit after all.
Once in orbit, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites one by one at an altitude of roughly 269 km (161 miles).
"All 26 Starlink V3 operational satellites deployed and operating nominally," Musk wrote on X.
Starship was built to launch SpaceX's Starlink satellites more frequently and carry future NASA missions to the moon. Reaching orbit, a primary benchmark for any new rocket designed to deliver payloads to space, was a long-delayed feat for Starship, which Musk once predicted would be achieved in 2022, to be followed by satellite deployments in 2023.
All 13 of Starship's previous test flights since 2023 were limited to suborbital space, despite a nearly decade-long development campaign that has cost SpaceX more than $15 billion to date. Musk has said he envisions ultimately flying hundreds or thousands of Starship missions a year, a launch pace unprecedented in the space industry.
"Starship is 2 to 3 years away from hourly flights," Musk wrote on X on Sunday.
Starship had been due to complete six Earth orbits on Monday before the mission was shortened. The engine issue on Monday made even more critical the mission objective of a successful deorbit, requiring a firing of one Raptor engine while in space to precisely angle the vehicle for atmospheric re-entry. The ship has three main Raptor engines.
Monday's voyage counts as the 14th test flight of Starship. But it nonetheless was carrying the group of new Starlink internet satellites, the first orbital payload for Starship.
Analysts estimate Monday's launch of SpaceX's new V3 Starlink satellites equals hundreds of millions of dollars in projected revenue for the company's Starlink unit, based on the network's added customer capacity - underscoring Starship's fundamental role in serving the company's profit nucleus.
According to SpaceX, the V3 Starlink satellites on Monday's mission can handle 10 times more data than their predecessor V2 mini-sats that the company has been launching 20 or 30 at a time on its workhorse Falcon 9 rockets.
Seeking to build out his broadband satellite constellation at a faster pace, Musk wants to launch the higher-capacity V3s in batches of 60 per launch once Starship goes into routine operation.
Starship's planned orbital debut also comes three months after SpaceX went public with a record-shattering IPO in June that made it the sixth-biggest US company by value and turned Musk, who founded the company in 2002, into the world's first trillionaire.
Much of SpaceX's market worth and continued investor confidence in the company - valued at $2 trillion as of Friday's close - rides on the success of Starship, which was designed as the world's first fully reusable spacecraft.
Starship is also set to play a pivotal role in Nasa's Artemis program, which aims to return astronauts to the moon's surface for the first time since 1972 and build a long-term lunar presence as a stepping stone to eventual human exploration of Mars.
Additional reporting by agencies
